B07_00: The receptor tyrosine kinase MET is coupled at focal adhesions to tensin proteins, linking the growth factor signal to how a cell grips and pulls on its substrate. It associates with tensin family members whose expression tends to be reciprocal: TNS4 stabilises the receptor and favours motility, while TNS3 predominates otherwise. Because tensins bridge the beta-1 integrin tail to actin, this places receptor signalling onto the adhesion machinery.
B07_01: Neuropilins are short-tailed cell-surface receptors with no kinase activity of their own that bind selected VEGF family ligands and present them to signalling VEGF receptors. NRP1 captures the heparin-binding VEGF-A165 plus VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 also binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both associate laterally with KDR or FLT1 to raise affinity for particular ligands, giving isoform-selective control of proliferation, migration and sprouting.
B07_02: Ligand binding dimerises and autophosphorylates the EGF receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling.
B07_03: Ligand binding to the KDR receptor triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation of its tail, recruiting and activating phospholipase C gamma; the inositol trisphosphate produced opens IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium that, with calmodulin, cooperates with diacylglycerol to activate conventional protein kinase C isoforms. PKC then feeds the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade, acting on Raf directly or relieving GTPase-activating protein restraint of Ras.
B07_04: One major branch downstream of the activated MET receptor tyrosine kinase runs through PI3K to AKT. Autophosphorylated MET recruits GRB2, which brings the multi-site adaptor GAB1 to the receptor; MET then phosphorylates GAB1 to create docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1. The associated PIK3CA catalytic subunit converts PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, recruiting AKT, which suppresses pro-apoptotic effectors and promotes mTOR-dependent growth.
B07_05: The receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4 can signal directly in the nucleus. Ligand binding to juxtamembrane-A isoforms triggers ectodomain shedding by ADAM17, then gamma-secretase cleavage liberating a soluble intracellular domain. This fragment escorts transcription factors into the nucleus and acts as their co-factor, repressing some targets with TAB2 and the corepressor NCOR1 and activating others with STAT5A or estrogen receptor; WW-domain partners YAP1 and WWOX set whether it arrives.
B07_06: Signalling through the ERBB4 receptor tyrosine kinase is terminated by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of the receptor and its cleavage fragments. WW-domain-binding motifs in the cytoplasmic tail recruit the NEDD4-family E3 ligases WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4, which ubiquitinate intact receptor and its membrane-anchored and soluble products, routing them to proteasomal and lysosomal degradation. Ubiquitination of the soluble fragment limits the pool entering the nucleus.
B07_07: Ligand binding dimerises the EGF receptor and triggers phosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tail. The adaptor GRB2 docks on those phosphotyrosines through its SH2 domain while holding the exchange factor SOS1 through its SH3 domains, so receptor occupancy delivers SOS1 to the membrane beside HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, where it promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange. Active RAS then feeds the MAP kinase cascade and transcriptional programmes for growth.
B07_08: When ERBB2 partners with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 after ligand binding, it also steers cell movement rather than only proliferation. Dimerisation and phosphorylation create a docking site for MEMO1, which holds active RHOA and its effector DIAPH1, a formin, at the plasma membrane. Actin polymerisation and microtubule capture are thereby coordinated at the leading edge, giving directed protrusion and stabilised polarity.
B07_09: Signalling begins when a secreted VEGF family ligand binds a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairs up, initiating cascades for proliferation, survival, migration and increased permeability. VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor, VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly homodimerise. KDR carries most signalling output while FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor.
B07_10: One branch of ERBB4 receptor output recruits phosphoinositide 3-kinase. Ligands including the neuregulins, betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF drive receptor dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation. Only the CYT1 splice isoforms retain the C-terminal tyrosine that docks the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 alpha; the p110 alpha catalytic subunit is then recruited, and the assembled kinase converts PIP2 to PIP3 to activate AKT, so splicing determines whether this coupling exists.
B07_11: Activation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase takes two steps. Its ligand is secreted as an inert single-chain precursor and must be cleaved by a membrane-anchored serine protease such as hepsin or by the activator HGFAC, with the Kunitz-domain inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restraining those proteases. Mature ligand then engages the SEMA and PSI domains of MET, promoting pairing and trans-autophosphorylation that creates adaptor docking sites.
B07_12: MET activates focal adhesion kinase only when PTK2 is engaged simultaneously by the receptor and by integrins contacting extracellular matrix, coupling a soluble growth factor cue to the adhesive state of the cell; SRC phosphorylation is required for full activity. The matrix side is supplied by fibronectin, collagens and laminin chains, read out through collagen- and laminin-binding integrins paired with beta1. The output is adhesion turnover and directed migration.
B07_13: After ligand binding, the activated MET receptor is internalised, and its endosomal route determines signal duration and strength: recycling to the plasma membrane sustains ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 output, while diverting it toward degradation shortens the response. Endocytosed receptor is sorted by the adaptor GGA3 through RAB4-marked recycling endosomes and returned with help from ARF6, while GRB2, GAB1 and CRK/CRKL stay bound and keep signalling from the endosome.
B07_14: In one branch downstream of the activated MET receptor tyrosine kinase, STAT3 docks at a phosphorylated tyrosine in the receptor carboxy-terminal tail, directly or via a scaffold, and is itself phosphorylated on Y705. That phosphorylation, to which SRC activity contributes, allows dimerisation, nuclear entry and target gene expression, and continued signalling from endosomes after internalisation sustains it. The output is anchorage-independent proliferation and increased motility.
B07_15: Growth signalling through the ERBB2:ERBB3 heterodimer is limited by negative feedback setting how much ERBB3 remains at the cell surface. Ligand binding to ERBB3 and pairing with ERBB2 activates AKT, which phosphorylates and stabilises the deubiquitinase USP8, reversing self-ubiquitination of the E3 ligase RNF41. Stabilised RNF41 then ubiquitinates ERBB3 for degradation, so receptor output limits its own duration; low RNF41 raises ligand sensitivity.
B07_16: Ligand-activated EGFR is removed from the cell surface and destroyed so signalling is limited in strength and duration. After autophosphorylation, the RING ubiquitin ligase CBL is recruited directly and through GRB2 and ubiquitinates the receptor. The adaptor SH3KBP1 links CBL to endophilins, which bend membranes during clathrin-coated pit formation, while EPS15 and epsin read the ubiquitin mark and HGS/STAM sort the cargo into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation.
B07_17: Ligand-bound EGFR pairs with ERBB2, and phospholipase C gamma 1 docks on specific phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails, notably EGFR Y992 and Y1173. Once recruited and activated, PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. The output feeds actin remodelling, migration and secretion, so receptor partner choice determines which second messengers a growth signal produces.
B07_18: One branch of MET receptor signalling reshapes the cytoskeleton by activating the small GTPases RAP1 and RAC1, producing scattering, lamellipodium formation, spreading and integrin-dependent adhesion. The activated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffold GAB1, whose phosphorylated tyrosines bind the adaptors CRK and CRKL. These dock exchange factors at the membrane: RAPGEF1 loads GTP onto RAP1A and RAP1B to strengthen adhesion, while DOCK7 acts on RAC1 to drive actin polymerisation.
B07_19: Much of the output of the activated MET receptor tyrosine kinase runs through RAS. The receptor does not contact RAS directly: phosphotyrosines on MET recruit the adaptors GRB2 and SHC1, or scaffolds such as RANBP9, which bring in the exchange factor SOS1 to catalyse GDP-to-GTP loading on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, and thence sustained ERK activity. Signalling continues from endosomes, and MUC20 or RANBP10 binding dampens it.
B07_20: Two drug classes converge on the ERBB2 receptor tyrosine kinase: small-molecule inhibitors that occupy the ATP-binding site and shut down catalytic activity, and monoclonal antibodies that bind the extracellular domain to prevent dimerisation and promote receptor downregulation. Loss of signalling removes proliferative and survival input to the PI3K/AKT and MAPK cascades. The chaperone HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 stabilises the receptor, while ERBIN binds and restrains it.
B07_21: Pharmacological inhibition blocks activation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase in two ways: monoclonal antibodies that intercept the ligand or occupy the receptor ectodomain and prevent ligand-induced dimerisation, and small-molecule inhibitors that block catalytic activity and downstream phosphorylation. The outcome is loss of receptor autophosphorylation and of the adaptor recruitment that would otherwise feed proliferative and motility signalling, including when the receptor signals excessively or without ligand.
B07_22: Ligand binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4 drives dimerisation and autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that dock the adaptor SHC1 through its phosphotyrosine-binding domain. ERBB4 then phosphorylates SHC1, creating a site for GRB2, which brings the exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane so that HRAS, KRAS or NRAS are loaded with GTP and the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade is engaged, converting receptor phosphorylation into proliferation, survival and differentiation signalling.
B07_23: After ligand binds its receptor and the complex is internalised, the hormone is destroyed while the receptor returns to the surface. The vacuolar ATPase, with its full complement of V0 and V1 subunits, pumps protons into the endosome, and the acidic pH releases the ligand for degradation by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D. Phosphatases such as PTP1B and PTPRF then dephosphorylate the activated kinase domain, terminating signalling.
B07_24: When ERBB2 heterodimerises with EGFR or ERBB4 after ligand binding, phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails become docking sites for the adaptor GRB2, converting ligand binding into RAS activation. GRB2 arrives bound to SOS1, an exchange factor that loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, which switches on RAF and the downstream MAP kinase cascade controlling cell cycle entry, growth and survival.
B07_25: The adaptor SHC1 provides one of two routes from ligand-bound EGFR to RAS activation. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated receptor tails through its SH2 and PTB domains, becomes tyrosine phosphorylated, and recruits GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, launching the MAPK cascade that drives proliferation, survival and migration. Any of the receptor's ligands can trigger it, several shed by proteolysis.
B07_26: PTK6 is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase activated downstream of ERBB2, linking receptor engagement at the plasma membrane to proliferation, migration and survival signalling. EGF-family and neuregulin ligands drive dimerisation of EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4, with ERBB2 the preferred heterodimer partner coupling these complexes to PTK6 activation. Because EGFR and MET also pair with ERBB2, signals apparently from them may be relayed through it instead.
B07_27: Ligand binding to ERBB3 drives formation of an ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimer, and phosphotyrosines in the ERBB3 tail create a docking site for the adaptor GRB7. GRB7 has no catalytic activity but links the complex to proliferative and migratory outputs: through SHC1 recruitment it contributes to RAS activation, and when phosphorylated by integrin-activated focal adhesion kinase it feeds VAV2-dependent RAC1 activation and cytoskeletal remodelling.
B07_28: Signalling through ERBB2 converges on the adaptor SHC1 to switch on RAS and the RAF/MAP kinase cascade. ERBB2 has no ligand of its own and acts as preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4, which bind EGF-family and neuregulin ligands; dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation create docking sites. SHC1 binds, is phosphorylated, and recruits GRB2 with SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS.
B07_29: One arm of VEGFR2 signalling loosens cell-cell junctions and relaxes surrounding smooth muscle. AKT, activated with PDPK1 and the mTORC2 components RICTOR and MLST8, phosphorylates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which with calmodulin, HSP90 and caveolin-1 releases nitric oxide. In parallel, VAV proteins activate RAC1 and the PAK kinases to trigger endocytosis of VE-cadherin, dismantling the adherens junction with its catenin and plakoglobin partners and opening the paracellular route.
B07_30: Signal attenuation returns a stimulated cell to baseline after a hormone pulse. Once ligand and receptor dissociate inside the endosome and the ligand is degraded there, endosome-associated tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphate from the activated receptor and its docking substrates. Dephosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 releases the adaptors GRB2 and SHC1 and the exchange factor SOS1, so the complexes feeding the ERK arm fall apart, with GRB10 adding further restraint.
B07_31: This branch routes ERBB2-containing heterodimer output into the PI3K-AKT axis. Neuregulins bind ERBB3 or ERBB4 and EGF-family ligands bind EGFR, driving heterodimerisation with ERBB2 and phosphorylation of the receptor tails. The p85 regulatory subunit docks directly on phosphorylated ERBB3 or ERBB4 CYT1 tails, or indirectly via GRB2 and GAB1 when the partner is EGFR, recruiting p110 to generate PIP3 and activate AKT.
B07_32: Assembly of the GAB1 signalosome converts EGF receptor stimulation into a lipid signal that activates AKT. Ligand-activated EGFR binds GRB2, which brings in the scaffold GAB1, and GAB1 recruits the PI3K subunits PIK3R1 and PIK3CA. The assembled complex phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, triggering AKT-dependent proliferation and resistance to apoptosis; GAB1 also docks the phosphatase PTPN11 and links to SRC-family activity restrained by CSK.
B07_33: One branch of activated MET receptor output runs through the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN11. Autophosphorylated MET recruits GRB2, which brings in the multisubstrate adaptor GAB1; GAB1 docks PTPN11 at the receptor complex, where it is itself tyrosine phosphorylated after stimulation. PTPN11 recruited this way sustains ERK1/2 activation and supports recruitment of sphingosine kinase, linking receptor engagement to lipid second messenger production, while also dephosphorylating receptor tyrosines and so limiting the signal.
B07_34: The activated insulin receptor recruits the docking proteins IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors for PI3K-dependent and Ras-MAP kinase output. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output.
